strengths: Targets a real and underexplored problem: controllable editing of explicit meshes, where most existing generative editing work is limited to implicit representations (NeRF/3DGS). The motivation for mesh-level editing in practical 3D pipelines is well argued.

The proposed Poisson Geometry Blending (Eq. 4–5) is a sensible adaptation of Poisson image editing to normal maps, and the hybrid SDF/Mesh optimization provides a principled way to absorb multi-view inconsistent blended normals while keeping unedited vertices frozen — this is the most technically interesting part of the paper.

Both components are ablated (Table 2, Fig. 6), including per-loss-term ablations of the texture harmonization, and the ablation table shows each module contributes; the baseline (plain mesh Boolean) is a fair reference point.

The framework is model-agnostic (FLUX Kontext, MeshyAI, MagicClay backbone are swappable), runs fast (~6 min on a 4090), and is extended to drag-based editing (Fig. 5), demonstrating versatility beyond text prompts.
Limitations are honestly stated (dependence on off-the-shelf generative models; difficulty with open/multi-layer/noisy meshes), and code release is promised.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients are all existing — MagicClay's hybrid SDF/mesh optimization is adopted wholesale as the backbone, Poisson image editing is applied off-the-shelf (Pérez et al.) to normal maps, and the pipeline structure (edit 2D image → lift to 3D → fuse) is conceptually close to prior work (MaskedLRM, MVEdit, Instant3dit, SeamlessNeRF, 3D Gaussian stitching). The claim of being 'the first framework' for this pipeline is overstated; the contribution is largely a system integration plus a Poisson-normal-blending loss.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: only 6 objects and a handful of editing tasks, 3 baselines, and no human user study despite the paper's central claims being about perceptual fidelity, 'harmonious' structure, and high-fidelity appearance. NIQE/NIMA computed on rendered mesh views are weak proxies for editing quality and their exact rendering protocol (views, lighting, resolution) is unspecified. The very large CLIPdir gap (13.59 vs 8.22 for the best baseline) and how the metric was normalized are not explained.

Several key methodological details are missing, hurting reproducibility and even assessability: values or selection procedure for λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, ε0, ε1, δ, σ, γ are not reported; how the edited region mesh Mr is registered/aligned to the original mesh Mo is not described (this alignment is critical and non-trivial); 'extract the components within the editing region' is vague — it is unclear whether manual 3D region specification is needed, which would undercut the claimed advantage over methods like FocalDreamer.

The texture harmonization is labeled 'Poisson' but is not a Poisson formulation: Ldistribution (KDE comparison evaluated at sample points, Eq. 7–8) is a rather ad hoc and statistically weak distribution-matching objective, and Lgrad/Lboundary are conventional losses. The naming overstates the technical connection.

Comparison fairness concerns: SDS-based baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay) were arguably designed for different edit types and may not be optimally prompted; Fig. 4 marks baseline results as 'Fail' without explaining what failure criterion was applied, and there is no discussion of failure cases of CraftMesh itself.

The claimed PBR material support is asserted in Sec. 3.2.2 but never evaluated with any experiment; the multi-view consistency issue of blended normal maps is handled only empirically ('the implicit SDF effectively resolves inconsistencies') without analysis of when this fails.

Reproducibility is questionable: the pipeline depends on the commercial MeshyAI API as an essential component, and no code or dataset release exists at submission time, so the 6-object evaluation set cannot be verified.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: controllable, locality-preserving editing of explicit meshes, an area that is underexplored relative to NeRF/3DGS editing, and meshes dominate professional content-creation pipelines.

The core idea of transferring Poisson Image Editing from RGB space to rendered normal maps (Poisson Geometry Blending) and to an implicit color field (Poisson Texture Harmonization) is a sensible and elegant reuse of a classical tool, and the ablations (Fig. 6, Tab. 2) show each loss term and module contributes.
The pipeline is modular and model-agnostic (any 2D editor, any image-to-mesh generator), and the drag-based editing extension (Sec. 4.4) demonstrates flexibility beyond text-driven edits.

Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 4 are visually convincing on complex edits (e.g., adding wings/tails, deleting a volcano) where baselines like FocalDreamer, MagicClay, and Instant3dit visibly fail or produce coarse geometry.
Runtime is modest (~6 minutes per edit on a single 4090), which is favorable compared to SDS-based iterative optimization methods.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to prior work: the hybrid SDF/Mesh representation, vertex optimization, and regularization losses are adopted directly from MagicClay [2], the geometry supervision is classical Poisson Image Editing [37], and the edited-region meshes come entirely from off-the-shelf components (FLUX Kontext [18], MeshyAI [32]). The contribution reduces to adapting PIE to normal maps and adding three texture losses, which is incremental.

The evaluation is far too narrow to support the 'outperforms state-of-the-art' claim: only six objects with a handful of edit types per object, and quantitative results aggregate over this tiny set with no statistical detail, per-task breakdown, or significance analysis.

The chosen metrics are weak proxies: CLIPsim/CLIPdir on rendered views are known to be unreliable for 3D editing fidelity, and NIQE/NIMA are 2D image-quality estimators that say little about geometric quality or 3D consistency. No user study is provided, which is standard practice for generative editing papers and would be the most appropriate evidence here.

Comparison fairness is unclear and possibly favorable to the authors: their method is conditioned on an edited reference image, while it is not specified what target-view images or prompts the baselines received; the very large CLIPdir gap (13.59 vs 2.20 for MagicClay) suggests conditions differ substantially rather than a pure method advantage. Baseline 'Fail' entries appear in Fig. 4 without explanation, while no failure cases of CraftMesh are shown.

Reproducibility is significantly undermined by dependence on the proprietary MeshyAI web service, and by missing hyperparameters: λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, ε0, ε1, δ, γ, and σ are never specified, nor are the number of random viewpoints, the alignment procedure for Me with Mt (Eq. 1–2 assumes pre-alignment without describing how it is done), or how the editing region for part extraction is selected in 3D.

Several methodological choices are heuristic and under-justified: the per-view blended normal maps np are admittedly not multi-view consistent, and the claim that 'the implicit SDF effectively resolves inconsistencies' is asserted rather than analyzed; the texture distribution loss (Eq. 7–8) matches RGB histograms globally, which cannot guarantee spatially plausible harmonization and could impose the wrong palette in edits with intentionally different colors.

The claim of being 'the first framework that reformulates mesh editing as an image editing–mesh generation–seamless fusion pipeline' overstates novelty; composing 2D editing with image-to-3D lifting followed by region fusion is a natural strategy others have explored in adjacent forms (e.g., Gao et al. [14] for Gaussians, SeamlessNeRF [15]).

Writing quality needs work: grammatical errors ('it's optimization region', 'The newly edited synthesized of the merged mesh'), an incomplete sentence ending 'oversimplified or distorted results' (missing period, Sec. 1), stray layout text in figures ('另外一栏' artifacts visible in Figs. 2, 3, 5, 6), and a missing Eq. (4) rendering context, indicating the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

strengths: The paper targets an underexplored problem: generative editing of explicit, textured meshes, as opposed to the many NeRF/3DGS editing works, which is a practically relevant direction for professional 3D content pipelines.

The overall pipeline (2D image editing -> image-to-mesh generation of an edited-region mesh -> fusion into the original mesh) is sensible and clearly motivated; it sidesteps the spatial controllability problems of SDS-based editing and the consistency problems of MVD-based editing.

Poisson Geometry Blending is a reasonable and somewhat novel adaptation: applying 2D Poisson Image Editing to blended normal maps as multi-view guidance, with the implicit SDF resolving the inherent multi-view inconsistency of per-view blended normals. This is a coherent technical idea.

The Poisson Texture Harmonization module (distribution-aware color alignment, gradient-preserving fusion, distance-weighted boundary loss) addresses a real failure mode (color shift and seams between generated and preserved regions) and the loss-term ablations in Fig. 6 qualitatively demonstrate each term's role.

Ablation results (Table 2) show each component individually improves over the Boolean-only baseline, and the combination yields the best numbers, giving some internal evidence that the proposed modules matter.

The drag-based editing extension (Sec. 4.4) demonstrates the framework's flexibility beyond text prompts, and the reported runtimes (a few minutes on a single 4090) are attractive compared to SDS optimization methods.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the core machinery — the hybrid SDF/mesh representation, indirect SDF optimization, vertex splitting/collapsing, smoothness and Eikonal regularization — is explicitly adopted from MagicClay [2] ('inspired by [2]', 'We adopt MagicClay [2] as the backbone'). The genuinely new elements reduce to (i) applying 2D Poisson Image Editing to normal maps as guidance and (ii) three relatively standard texture-space losses. The framing as the 'first framework' for this pipeline is an overclaim given prior 2D-edit + 3D-generation editing systems.

Very small evaluation set: quantitative results are averaged over only six objects. CLIP-based averages over six samples are highly noisy, and six objects cannot support the claim of 'outperforming state-of-the-art methods' in general. No user study is provided, so perceptual claims ('aesthetically satisfying to human vision') rest on NIQE/NIMA and author-selected qualitative examples.

Concerns about fairness of the quantitative comparison: baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit) are fundamentally different paradigms evaluated with official implementations, but the reported CLIPdir gaps are implausibly large (e.g., 13.59 vs. 8.22/2.20/2.08). It is unclear whether the baselines were tuned or conditioned comparably; the paper does not report per-task or per-object breakdowns that would allow scrutiny.

Significant reproducibility limitations: the pipeline depends on closed-source/commercial components (FLUX Kontext, the MeshyAI commercial API) and on MagicClay's internals. Even with code release, exact reproduction would hinge on proprietary APIs and unstated hyperparameters — λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, ε0, ε1, δ, σ, γ are all unspecified.

The ablation baseline is merely a raw mesh Boolean operation, which is a weak reference; an ablation against, e.g., vertex-optimization-based blending without the SDF, or PIE applied to rendered images rather than normal maps, would better isolate the contribution.

Several methodological details are under-specified: how the SDF is 'bound' to the mesh during vertex optimization, how the edited reference mesh Me is aligned to Mt, how regions are selected/extracted from the edited reference mesh, and how the optional second image-editing step affects results. Eq. (8) also appears to compare density values rather than distributions in a clearly principled way, and the statement about PBR extension (Sec. 3.2.2) is asserted without any supporting experiment.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammatical problems (e.g., 'it's optimization region', 'The newly edited synthesized of the merged mesh Mt lack texture information'), and some claims in the qualitative section are difficult to verify from the small rendered crops in Fig. 4.

The limitation section honestly acknowledges dependence on off-the-shelf generators, but this also means the observed quality gains may largely reflect the strength of the substituted generative backbones rather than the fusion framework itself; a same-backbone controlled comparison is not provided.

strengths: Addresses an underserved and practically important problem: generative editing of explicit surface meshes, which is the dominant representation in professional 3D content pipelines, whereas most prior work targets implicit representations.

The image editing–mesh generation–seamless fusion pipeline is a sensible reframing that sidesteps the multi-view consistency and structure-preservation failures of SDS- and MVD-based editing approaches, and it supports both text-driven and drag-driven editing (Fig. 5), demonstrating versatility.

The Poisson Geometry Blending idea—applying classical Poisson Image Editing to blend normal maps rendered from the edited region and original meshes, then supervising an SDF with the blended normals—is a clean and computationally attractive way to obtain smooth geometric transitions (O(kn^2) in 2D rather than O(n^3) volumetric solving).

Experiments are reasonably broad: 100 models from mixed sources, insertion/deletion/localized editing tasks, comparison against four recent baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit, VoxHammer), component-level ablations with qualitative evidence (Fig. 6), and a backend-swap ablation (Trellis, Hunyuan3D 2.5, MeshyAI) that partially supports the claim that gains come from the fusion pipeline rather than a specific generative backbone.
The paper is clearly written and well organized; the method section is specific enough to understand the overall algorithm, and runtime figures (6 min total on a 4090) suggest practicality.
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty. The framework is largely a system-level integration of off-the-shelf components (FLUX Kontext for editing, MeshyAI/Trellis/Hunyuan3D for generation, MagicClay's hybrid SDF/mesh representation as the optimization backbone). The two 'core techniques' adapt classical Poisson Image Editing [38] to normal maps and to texture space; the texture losses (gradient consistency, nearest-point boundary loss, KDE-based distribution matching) are fairly standard heuristics rather than a principled new formulation.

Potential unfairness in the main quantitative comparison (Table 1). The proposed method uses a state-of-the-art proprietary image editor (FLUX Kontext) and a strong commercial image-to-mesh generator (MeshyAI), while baselines rely on their own weaker backbones. The large CLIPdir gap (18.5 vs. 10.5 for the next best) may substantially reflect better 2D/3D generative models rather than the fusion contribution; the paper only partially disentangles this via backend ablations and never reports baselines with upgraded backends.

The ablation study (Table 2) is internally inconsistent with its own claims. There is no row combining Geometry Blending and Texture Harmonization on the same backend, so the claim that 'combining them yields the best performance' is not actually shown; the 'Ours' rows instead conflate the two modules with a backbone change. The jump in CLIPdir from ~11–12 (component ablations) to ~18.5–18.9 (full method with different backends) is unexplained.

Several technical details are questionable or under-specified: (a) the boundary weight w_i = (1 - δ/||p_new - p_pr||)^2 grows without bound as the point distance approaches zero, which seems pathological for a loss meant to be distance-attenuated; (b) the sigmoid on numerically estimated color gradients in Eq. (7) is ad hoc; (c) multi-view inconsistency of the blended normal maps is acknowledged but the claim that the SDF 'resolves' it is asserted rather than analyzed; (d) hyperparameters (ε0, ε1, δ, γ, σ, λ's, θ's) and camera setups are not reported.

No user study, despite the paper's emphasis on perceptual quality and 'harmony'; CLIP-based metrics and no-reference IQA (NIQE/NIMA) are known to be weak proxies for mesh editing quality, and the reported NIQE values are not contextualized.

Reproducibility is weak: the project page field is empty, no code or data release is mentioned, and the evaluation set mixes Objaverse-XL, Google Scanned Objects, and unspecified 'internet' models without release plans.

The limitation section is thin: dependence on Boolean operations implies the method requires watertight, well-conditioned inputs, and failure modes of the 2D editing→3D lifting step (e.g., edits invisible from a single reference view) are not characterized or quantified.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem—controllable, part-level editing of explicit meshes—which is under-explored relative to neural-field editing, and meshes are the dominant representation in production pipelines.

The image editing → region mesh generation → Poisson fusion decomposition is a sensible, flexible design that sidesteps the multi-view consistency issues of SDS/MVD-based editing, and the pipeline is model-agnostic (demonstrated with Trellis, Hunyuan3D, and MeshyAI backends).

The Poisson Geometry Blending idea of applying 2D Poisson Image Editing to rendered normal maps as guidance for SDF optimization is a neat reuse of a classical tool that reduces a 3D volumetric problem to O(kn²), with a plausible motivation for why gradient-domain blending is preferable to coordinate-domain Poisson mesh editing.
Ablations cover each loss term (distribution, gradient, boundary) and both fusion modules, and the drag-based editing extension (Sec. 4.4) shows some versatility.
Reported runtimes (5 min geometry, 1 min texture on a single 4090) suggest the method is practical.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the framework is largely an assembly of off-the-shelf components—FLUX Kontext for image editing, MeshyAI/Hunyuan3D/Trellis for image-to-mesh, MagicClay's hybrid SDF/mesh representation and losses (the paper explicitly adopts MagicClay as 'the backbone'), mesh Booleans, and classical Poisson Image Editing. The core new technical contribution reduces to applying PIE to normal maps and three texture losses, which reads as incremental engineering rather than a substantive methodological advance.

The evaluation does not convincingly isolate the paper's contribution. In Table 2, the Boolean-only baseline already achieves 17.723 CLIPsim / 10.348 CLIPdir—comparable to or better than VoxHammer in Table 1 (17.366 / 10.482)—suggesting that much of the reported gain comes from modern generative backends rather than the proposed fusion. Moreover, the ablation is internally confusing: 'w/ Geometry Blending' and 'w/ Texture Harmonization' rows score ~11–12 CLIPdir while the full method scores ~18.5–18.9, an unexplained jump given that the full method is supposedly the combination of the two; the ablation rows and the full-method rows also appear to use different backends, undermining the claimed attribution of improvement to the fusion pipeline.

No user study or perceptual evaluation with humans; CLIPsim/CLIPdir are computed on a single rendered view (the exact view is unspecified), and NIQE/NIMA are generic 2D no-reference metrics of questionable validity for 3D mesh editing. These metrics favor methods whose outputs resemble high-quality internet imagery rather than measuring edit quality, boundary seams, or preservation of untouched geometry.

A fundamental limitation is under-addressed: the 2D edit is performed on a single reference image and the region mesh is generated from essentially one view. Multi-view consistency of the edited region (both geometry and texture) with the original mesh from unseen viewpoints is not quantified or thoroughly discussed—the paper concedes blended normal maps are 'not strictly multi-view consistent' but provides no analysis of when this fails. Qualitative figures show only one canonical view.

Reproducibility is weak: the 'Project page' link in the paper is empty, no code or dataset release is stated, and key hyperparameters (λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, ε0, ε1, δ, γ, camera setup, number of views, iteration counts per stage) are not specified. The evaluation dataset construction ('selecting from Objaverse-XL, Google Scanned Objects and the internet') is too vague to reproduce, and the prompts/ground truth are not released.

Baseline fairness concerns: comparisons are against older SDS-based methods (FocalDreamer, MagicClay) and early MVD approaches, while the proposed method benefits from state-of-the-art 2024–2025 generators. A stronger control—e.g., Boolean fusion + direct texture generation without the proposed Poisson losses, or replacing MagicClay's guidance with the proposed normal blending using identical backends—would be needed to substantiate claims of state-of-the-art fusion quality.

Several method details are underspecified or questionable: how the 'editing region' is extracted from the edited reference mesh (segmentation? user annotation?) is not explained; Eq. (7)'s sigmoid-scaled gradient MSE is only loosely connected to the claimed PIE formulation; the distribution loss in Eq. (11) compares KDE densities at sample points in a way whose behavior is not analyzed (bandwidth sensitivity, high-dimensional RGB sample sparsity).

Writing quality issues: typos ('Specifically, We propose'), empty figure placeholders/text fragments, and duplicated notation (M_t^in defined twice, inconsistent sub/superscripts across Eqs. 1–3) make the technical exposition harder to follow than it should be.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and under-explored problem: generative editing of explicit surface meshes, which is more relevant to professional 3D content pipelines than implicit/NeRF-based editing.

The core idea is elegant and well-motivated: performing Poisson image editing on rendered normal maps reduces 3D volumetric Poisson fusion (O(n^3)) to a 2D problem (O(kn^2)) while using the hybrid SDF/Mesh representation to resolve per-view inconsistencies. This is a sensible re-use of a classical tool in a new domain.

The pipeline is model-agnostic: the authors demonstrate the fusion framework with three different mesh generation backends (MeshyAI, Hunyuan3D 2.5, Trellis), which supports the claim that improvements come from the fusion stage rather than a particular generator.

Reasonably broad experimental protocol: 100 diverse 3D models from multiple sources, three editing prompts each, covering insertion, deletion, and localized edits; comparisons against four recent baselines including the training-free VoxHammer.

Additional demonstration of drag-based mesh editing via LightningDrag shows the flexibility of the image-editing–mesh-generation–fusion decomposition, and ablations qualitatively isolate each proposed loss (distribution, gradient, boundary).
Practical runtimes (roughly 6 minutes total on a single 4090) make the method usable in interactive workflows.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the geometry fusion essentially applies classical Poisson Image Editing [38] to normal maps, and the hybrid SDF/mesh optimization backbone, smoothness/Eikonal losses are adopted directly from MagicClay [2]. The main contributions are pipeline assembly and two loss functions; the claimed novelty of 'solving the Poisson equation on the gradient domain' is somewhat overstated relative to what is actually standard 2D PIE on normal maps.

The quantitative evaluation relies on CLIPsim, CLIPdir, NIQE, and NIMA computed from renders. These are known to be weak proxies for editing fidelity—CLIP metrics can reward plausible generation rather than faithful local edits—and the very large CLIPdir margin (18.5 vs. 10.5 for the best baseline) is suspicious and unvalidated. No human/user study is provided to substantiate the 'high-fidelity' and 'harmonious' claims.

The ablation in Table 2 is confounded and internally inconsistent: 'w/ Geometry Blending' (CLIPdir 11.979) and 'w/ Texture Harmonization' (10.724) are far below 'Ours' (18.479), and the backend rows (Hunyuan3D 2.5, Trellis) reach ~18.6–18.9 CLIPdir regardless of module combination. It is unclear whether the two ablation rows use the same generation backend, and NIQE actually degrades for the Hunyuan3D and Trellis configurations relative to the baseline, undermining the 'consistently best' narrative.

Technical soundness concerns are under-addressed: blending normal maps per-view is not multi-view consistent, and the paper only asserts that 'the implicit SDF effectively resolves inconsistencies' without analysis, failure cases, or conditions under which this holds. Alignment between Mo, Mt, and Me via [58] is stated in one sentence without error analysis.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, the 'project page' is blank, hyperparameters (λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, δ, γ, ε0, ε1, σ, number of views, camera setup) are unspecified, and the dataset construction ('selecting from the internet') is vague with no release plan.

Presentation flaws: Eq. (1) is missing (equations jump to (2)), there are typos ('Specifically, We propose'), parts of Fig. 2 are illegible, and the 'Fail' rows in Fig. 4 are shown for baselines but the paper does not discuss its own failure modes beyond a generic limitation paragraph.

The comparison fairness is questionable: baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit) operate under different input assumptions (text vs. image conditions), and using substantially newer, more powerful off-the-shelf editors/generators (FLUX Kontext, MeshyAI) makes it hard to attribute gains to the fusion method rather than to stronger components—although the backend ablation partially mitigates this, the ablation design itself is unclear (see above).
